To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have generated a robust human blood brain barrier model using induced pluripotent cells.
we have developed a robust and physiologically relevant human BBB model comprising BMECs, neurons, and astrocytes derived from the same donor source of human iPSCs.

we have developed an isogenic human blood‐brain barrier model that consists of brain endothelial cells derived from human induced‐pluripotent stem cells, astrocyte, and neurons, and that this model exhibits the key properties of a human blood‐brain model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a robust and scalable in vitro BBB model that could be used for a wide variety of applications, including drug development, disease modeling, and toxicity testing.
the generation of an in vitro blood brain barrier model.
the generation of a novel human‐induced neural cell model of the BBB.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human iPSC‐generated BBB model provides a platform to study BBB physiology and disease in a human‐specific context.
the iPSC-derived neurons and astrocyte cells were able to induce barrier function in iPSC-derived BMECs, and that an isogenic multicelluar BBB model was successfully developed.

we have developed an in vitro model of the human blood‐brain barrier using human induced pluripotential stem cells that is capable of recapitulating the barrier properties of the in vivo human blood‐brain interface.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed a robust and isogenic BBB model comprising brain endothelium, astrocytes and neuronal cells derived from human iPSCs.
we have developed a human‐based in vitro BBB model that is comprised of cells derived from the same human source.

a human‐based in vitro model of the blood–brain barrier was developed that is comprised of human brain microvascular endothelium and human astrocytes and human neurons, and that this model is capable of recapitulating many of the key functional characteristics of the blood–blood barrier.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can generate an isogenic human BBB model from human iPSCs.
the human‐induced stem cell platform provides a powerful tool for the study of the BBB and its associated pathologies.
we have developed a novel human‐induced‐pluripotent‐stem cell (hiPSC)‐based blood–brain barrier platform that is amenable to the study of the neurovascular interactions in health and disease.
